young.html: Long ago, the Greeks told a story about a war. A Trojan prince named Paris carried off Helen, the wife of a Greek king, to his city of Troy. The Greeks sailed across the sea to bring her back, and they camped outside Troy's high walls for ten years.

The Iliad does not tell the whole war. It tells a few weeks near the end, and it is about one feeling: the anger of the greatest Greek fighter, Achilles. When the Greek leader Agamemnon insults him, Achilles refuses to fight. Without him the Greeks start to lose. Then Achilles' best friend, Patroclus, is killed by the Trojan hero Hector, and Achilles' anger turns into grief and revenge.

The poem is full of battles, and some of them are rough to read. The best parts for young readers are the quiet ones. Hector says goodbye to his wife and baby son on the city wall; the baby is frightened by the horsehair crest on his father's helmet, and Hector laughs and takes it off. At the very end, Hector's old father, King Priam, goes alone at night to Achilles' tent to ask for his son's body. Achilles thinks of his own father, and the two enemies weep together.

young.cap: Tap a book of the Iliad to see what happens in it. The line shows how Achilles' anger rises and changes.

young.html: Tell it like a bard. The Iliad was sung aloud for a long time before it was written down. Singers used repeated phrases to help them: "swift-footed Achilles", "Hector of the shining helmet", "rosy-fingered Dawn". Make up a repeated phrase for each person in your family ("Dad, maker of pancakes"), then tell the story of your morning using them. Did the phrases make it easier to keep going?

full.html: Nobody knows who Homer was. The Greeks believed he was a blind poet from Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey. Modern scholars agree on a few things: the Iliad grew out of a long tradition of oral poetry, sung by bards who learned the stories and the ways of telling them from older bards, and it reached something like its present form around 750 to 700 BC. It is in Greek hexameter verse, about 15,700 lines, later divided into 24 books.

The war it describes was set in the Bronze Age, centuries before Homer. Troy was a real city, at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey, excavated from 1870 on. It was destroyed more than once. How much of Homer's war happened is still argued over.

full.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.
full.author: Homer

full.html: The first word of the poem in Greek is mēnin, "wrath" or "anger". That is the subject. Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks (Homer calls them Achaeans, Argives or Danaans), must give back a captive woman to her father, a priest of Apollo, to end a plague. To make up for it he takes Briseis, the captive given to Achilles. Achilles withdraws from the fighting and asks his mother, the sea goddess Thetis, to have Zeus let the Trojans win until the Greeks see what they have lost.

full.cap: The Iliad's 24 books. Choose one to see its main events; the line traces Achilles' anger from the quarrel to the meeting with Priam.

head: Books
What happens
rows: The armies, a duel between Paris and Menelaus, the Greek hero Diomedes' great day, Hector's farewell to Andromache.
The Trojans drive the Greeks back to their ships. An embassy (Book 9) begs Achilles to return; he refuses.
Patroclus fights in Achilles' armor and is killed by Hector.
Achilles returns, with new armor made by the god Hephaestus, and kills Hector.
Funeral games for Patroclus; Priam ransoms Hector's body; Hector's funeral.

full.html: Homer gives the Trojans as much honor as the Greeks. Hector is fighting for his city, his wife and his son. In Book 6 he prays for the baby Astyanax:

full.text: "Jove," he cried, "grant that this my child may be even as myself, chief among the Trojans; let him be not less excellent in strength, and let him rule Ilius with his might. Then may one say of him as he comes from battle, 'The son is far better than the father.'"
full.author: Homer
full.note: Butler uses the Latin names of the gods: Jove for Zeus. Ilius is Troy.

full.html: The hero's choice. Achilles knows he has two possible fates: a short life with glory that lasts forever, or a long, quiet life that is forgotten. Glory (kleos) and honor (timē) drive the whole quarrel: Agamemnon's insult was an attack on Achilles' honor.
The poem does not end with the fall of Troy. It ends with two enemies. Priam, guided by the god Hermes, comes to Achilles' hut and kneels:

full.text: Think of your father, O Achilles like unto the gods, who is such even as I am, on the sad threshold of old age. … Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me, who am the more pitiable, for I have steeled myself as no man yet has ever steeled himself before me, and have raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son.
full.author: Homer

full.html: Achilles gives back the body and grants a truce for the funeral. His anger, which began the poem, ends in pity. The last line is about Hector's burial.

The Greeks learned to read on Homer. For a thousand years the Iliad was the shared book of the Greek world, quoted by philosophers, historians and generals. Plato, later on this ladder, both loved Homer and argued that his stories of quarreling gods were bad for the young.
Thinking the Iliad tells the Trojan horse story. It doesn't: the horse comes up briefly in the Odyssey and is told in full by Virgil in the Aeneid. The Iliad also ends before Achilles' death.

deep.html: Was there one Homer, or many? In 1795 the German scholar F. A. Wolf argued that the poems were stitched together from shorter songs. In the 1920s and 1930s the American scholar Milman Parry showed how the repeated epithets ("swift-footed Achilles") fit the meter like building blocks, the tools of a singer composing as he performs. With Albert Lord he recorded oral poets in Yugoslavia who could sing long epics this way. Most scholars now think the Iliad comes from that kind of tradition, shaped by one or more great poets, and fixed in writing at some point; when and how are still debated.

The Iliad is a war poem that never pretends war is simple. It gives the names and homes of the men who die, often with a line about the parents who will never see them again. Its long similes compare battle to storms, harvests and fires, reminding the listener of the peaceful world outside. The Shield of Achilles in Book 18 shows a city at peace with a wedding and a court case beside a city at war.

items: Is Achilles right to refuse to fight after he is insulted? When does pride become a fault?
Why does the poem end with Priam and Achilles instead of the fall of Troy?
Can a poem honor both sides of a war?
The gods take sides and quarrel. Does that make the human choices matter less, or more?

deep.html: Later books answer back. Virgil's Aeneid retells the war from the Trojan side. Plato's Republic questions what Homer teaches. Aristotle's Poetics praises Homer for giving the Iliad one unified action. Simone Weil's essay "The Iliad, or the Poem of Force" (1940) read it as a poem about what violence does to everyone it touches.

questions: Achilles stops fighting because his honor was hurt. Have you ever refused to help because you felt treated unfairly? How did it turn out?
Hector fights for his family and city even though he fears he will lose. Is that brave, or something else?
Why do you think Achilles gives Hector's body back to Priam?
Homer makes the enemy side human and sympathetic. Why might that be hard for people at war, and why might it matter?
The Iliad was sung and memorized for generations before it was written down. What stories in your family are passed on by telling, not by writing?
care: The Iliad has many vivid battle deaths. This lesson summarizes them without detail. For young readers, the farewell of Hector and Andromache (Book 6) and Priam's visit to Achilles (Book 24) are the best scenes to read together.
